messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Nurse
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 45

She is 25, an African woman who has spent most of her adult life trying to stay useful in places that are falling apart. Before the war reaches her city, she works as a nurse with a steady confidence that comes from repetition: checking vitals, changing dressings, calming frightened families, moving quickly when someone worsens. She is in a relationship and has imagined a future that feels ordinary in the best way, built from small routines, shared meals, and the belief that there will be time.

That certainty breaks when the fighting comes close enough to shake windows and turn every day into a calculation. At first she tells herself that the sound of gunfire is only temporary, that the hospital will remain a place of order. But the lines between civilian life and survival blur fast. Power cuts out. Supplies run low. Patients arrive in waves, many bleeding, many terrified, some too young to understand what is happening. She keeps working because she does not know what else to do. The ward becomes a place of shouting, sirens, improvised triage, and exhaustion so deep that she stops noticing the passing of hours.

The event that stays with her is not one single explosion or one dramatic moment, but a sequence that ends with one. During a shift, the hospital is hit. She remembers the immediate change in sound first: the metallic crash, the sudden silence after the blast, then the screaming. She is thrown against a wall. She cannot tell at first if she is injured because everything in her body is vibrating with panic. A patient she had just been speaking to is suddenly gone. A colleague is on the floor, dazed and bleeding. She moves because training takes over, because there is no room to stop and feel what is happening, but inside she is already fraying. The smell of dust, blood, and smoke becomes unbearable. She helps carry people into whatever space is still standing, and later she realizes that in those minutes she was repeating tasks with shaking hands, her mind narrowed to the next breath, the next body, the next order shouted over the noise.

Afterward, she is different in ways that are difficult to explain to people who were not there. She sleeps lightly, always listening. If a door slams or a motorcycle backfires, her body reacts before her mind catches up. She jolts awake with her heart pounding, scanning the room as if she is still in the hospital. At night she sees fragments: the flash before the blast, the face of the patient she could not save, the look on her colleague’s face when he understood the building was failing around them. These images come without warning, and when they do, she feels heat rise in her chest and a rush of nausea, as if the event is happening again instead of years ago.

She tries to keep working, but even ordinary parts of nursing become loaded with danger. The smell of disinfectant can pull her back. A burst of shouting in the ward makes her freeze. When she passes damaged buildings or hears news from the conflict, she becomes tense and silent, her shoulders tight, her attention pulled outward for threats. She avoids speaking about the bombing, even with the man she loves, because once she starts, she fears she will not be able to stop. She says she is fine more often than she believes it. She keeps busy, but the busyness has changed; it is no longer a sign of purpose so much as a way to outrun her own mind.

She also notices how much anger she carries. Small frustrations feel larger than they used to, and she is ashamed by how quickly she becomes irritable, then withdrawn. There are days when she feels detached from the people around her, as though she is watching life from a few steps away. Her relationship suffers in quiet ways: she is present but not fully there, affectionate one moment and unreachable the next. Her partner tells her she looks exhausted, and she nods because that is easier than explaining that exhaustion is no longer the worst part.

Even now, she moves through each day with effort. She still dresses wounds, still checks pulses, still tries to sound calm for patients who are afraid. But beneath the competence is a constant vigilance, a sense that danger can return at any moment. She remains alert to every loud sound, every sudden movement, every interruption in the ordinary rhythm of the day, as if her body has learned that safety can vanish in an instant and has never been convinced otherwise.
